case_info.scenario: A 51-year-old previously healthy man was admitted with severe neck pain for 6 days. In the past month, he felt neck stiffness, accompanied by swelling and persistent dull pain of the upper anterior chest wall, which could be transiently relieved by taking oral ibuprofen. Six days before admission, the patient’s neck stiffness transited to an endurable dull ache. When turning his head, there was severe burning pain in the posterior neck and occiput, followed immediately by an electric shocklike numbness on ipsilateral side tongue, which led to a forced head position. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine with gadolinium on admission revealed signal abnormality in C1/C2 vertebrae (Figure 1A). In the past 3 days, with the intensification of neck pain, the patient found pustules on both hands, which gradually increased. He had no history of tobacco, alcohol, or drug misuse. On examination, he was afebrile. There was tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation, upper neck, post aurem, and occiput. Multiple pustules were seen in the palm and back of both hands (Figure 1B). Complete blood cell count and liver and kidney function yielded normal results, except for elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 93 mm/h and C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 5.5 mg/dL (to convert to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10). Results of workup for rheumatic and infectious disease, including antinuclear, antineutrophil cytoplasmic and anticardiolipin antibodies, human leukocyte antigen B27, repeated blood cultures, rapid plasma reagin test, Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, brucella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and rickettsial antibodies, were all negative. Cell count, protein, and glucose in cerebrospinal fluid were normal. Cultures of cerebrospinal fluid revealed no organisms. Whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography revealed no malignancy.

case_info.explanation: D. Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. An association betweenCSF2RA,NOD2,MEGF6, andADAM5genes and the predisposition of SAPHO syndrome has been established.5Elevated serum IgG4 and some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL) 6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-23 and endothelin-1, have been described in patients with SAPHO syndrome.6In laboratory tests, and features of an active inflammatory process (accelerated ESR, elevated CRP) are observed.7 The diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome is based on fulfilling at least 1 of the criteria described by Kahn and Kahn,8which include (1) chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, usually sterile, spine may be involved, with or without skin lesions, (2) acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis associated with any of the following: palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), pustular psoriasis, or severe acne, and (3) any sterile osteitis associated with any of the following: PPP, pustular psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, or severe acne. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. Current treatment options for SAPHO syndrome include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, and biologics.10 After oral etoricoxib and prednisolone treatment, neck pain and pustules gradually subsided and ESR and CRP decreased. The patient has remained clinically stable at 6-month follow-up. Clinicians should be aware of this unusual syndrome to avoid misdiagnosis (tumor/infection), unnecessary surgery, and antibiotic therapy.

       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.

       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Abnormal enhancement of C1/C2 vertebrae with prevertebral and retrodental tissue as well as of the anterior vertebrae at C4/C5 with hyperostotic anterior osteophytes on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and multiple pustules on the palm (B).
case_info.explanation: D. Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. An association betweenCSF2RA,NOD2,MEGF6, andADAM5genes and the predisposition of SAPHO syndrome has been established.5Elevated serum IgG4 and some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL) 6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-23 and endothelin-1, have been described in patients with SAPHO syndrome.6In laboratory tests, and features of an active inflammatory process (accelerated ESR, elevated CRP) are observed.7 The diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome is based on fulfilling at least 1 of the criteria described by Kahn and Kahn,8which include (1) chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, usually sterile, spine may be involved, with or without skin lesions, (2) acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis associated with any of the following: palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), pustular psoriasis, or severe acne, and (3) any sterile osteitis associated with any of the following: PPP, pustular psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, or severe acne. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. case_info.caption: Abnormal enhancement of C1/C2 vertebrae with prevertebral and retrodental tissue as well as of the anterior vertebrae at C4/C5 with hyperostotic anterior osteophytes on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and multiple pustules on the palm (B).
case_info.explanation: D. Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. An association betweenCSF2RA,NOD2,MEGF6, andADAM5genes and the predisposition of SAPHO syndrome has been established.5Elevated serum IgG4 and some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL) 6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-23 and endothelin-1, have been described in patients with SAPHO syndrome.6In laboratory tests, and features of an active inflammatory process (accelerated ESR, elevated CRP) are observed.7 The diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome is based on fulfilling at least 1 of the criteria described by Kahn and Kahn,8which include (1) chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, usually sterile, spine may be involved, with or without skin lesions, (2) acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis associated with any of the following: palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), pustular psoriasis, or severe acne, and (3) any sterile osteitis associated with any of the following: PPP, pustular psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, or severe acne. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. Current treatment options for SAPHO syndrome include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, and biologics.10 After oral etoricoxib and prednisolone treatment, neck pain and pustules gradually subsided and ESR and CRP decreased. The patient has remained clinically stable at 6-month follow-up. Clinicians should be aware of this unusual syndrome to avoid misdiagnosis (tumor/infection), unnecessary surgery, and antibiotic therapy.

case_info.answer: Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome
case_info.caption: Abnormal enhancement of C1/C2 vertebrae with prevertebral and retrodental tissue as well as of the anterior vertebrae at C4/C5 with hyperostotic anterior osteophytes on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and multiple pustules on the palm (B).
case_info.explanation: D. Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. An association betweenCSF2RA,NOD2,MEGF6, andADAM5genes and the predisposition of SAPHO syndrome has been established.5Elevated serum IgG4 and some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL) 6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-23 and endothelin-1, have been described in patients with SAPHO syndrome.6In laboratory tests, and features of an active inflammatory process (accelerated ESR, elevated CRP) are observed.7 The diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome is based on fulfilling at least 1 of the criteria described by Kahn and Kahn,8which include (1) chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, usually sterile, spine may be involved, with or without skin lesions, (2) acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis associated with any of the following: palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), pustular psoriasis, or severe acne, and (3) any sterile osteitis associated with any of the following: PPP, pustular psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, or severe acne. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. Current treatment options for SAPHO syndrome include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, and biologics.10 After oral etoricoxib and prednisolone treatment, neck pain and pustules gradually subsided and ESR and CRP decreased. The patient has remained clinically stable at 6-month follow-up. Clinicians should be aware of this unusual syndrome to avoid misdiagnosis (tumor/infection), unnecessary surgery, and antibiotic therapy.

You are a deliberation POLICY steering a conversation between a medical AI and a clinician toward
the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop

case_info.answer: Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome
case_info.caption: Abnormal enhancement of C1/C2 vertebrae with prevertebral and retrodental tissue as well as of the anterior vertebrae at C4/C5 with hyperostotic anterior osteophytes on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and multiple pustules on the palm (B).
case_info.explanation: D. Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. An association betweenCSF2RA,NOD2,MEGF6, andADAM5genes and the predisposition of SAPHO syndrome has been established.5Elevated serum IgG4 and some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL) 6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-23 and endothelin-1, have been described in patients with SAPHO syndrome.6In laboratory tests, and features of an active inflammatory process (accelerated ESR, elevated CRP) are observed.7 The diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome is based on fulfilling at least 1 of the criteria described by Kahn and Kahn,8which include (1) chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, usually sterile, spine may be involved, with or without skin lesions, (2) acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis associated with any of the following: palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), pustular psoriasis, or severe acne, and (3) any sterile osteitis associated with any of the following: PPP, pustular psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, or severe acne. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. Current treatment options for SAPHO syndrome include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, and biologics.10 After oral etoricoxib and prednisolone treatment, neck pain and pustules gradually subsided and ESR and CRP decreased. The patient has remained clinically stable at 6-month follow-up. Clinicians should be aware of this unusual syndrome to avoid misdiagnosis (tumor/infection), unnecessary surgery, and antibiotic therapy.

A 51-year-old previously healthy man was admitted with severe neck pain for 6 days. In the past month, he felt neck stiffness, accompanied by swelling and persistent dull pain of the upper anterior chest wall, which could be transiently relieved by taking oral ibuprofen. Six days before admission, the patient’s neck stiffness transited to an endurable dull ache. When turning his head, there was severe burning pain in the posterior neck and occiput, followed immediately by an electric shocklike numbness on ipsilateral side tongue, which led to a forced head position. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine with gadolinium on admission revealed signal abnormality in C1/C2 vertebrae (Figure 1A). In the past 3 days, with the intensification of neck pain, the patient found pustules on both hands, which gradually increased. He had no history of tobacco, alcohol, or drug misuse. On examination, he was afebrile. There was tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation, upper neck, post aurem, and occiput. Multiple pustules were seen in the palm and back of both hands (Figure 1B). Complete blood cell count and liver and kidney function yielded normal results, except for elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 93 mm/h and C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 5.5 mg/dL (to convert to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10). Results of workup for rheumatic and infectious disease, including antinuclear, antineutrophil cytoplasmic and anticardiolipin antibodies, human leukocyte antigen B27, repeated blood cultures, rapid plasma reagin test, Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, brucella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and rickettsial antibodies, were all negative. Cell count, protein, and glucose in cerebrospinal fluid were normal. Cultures of cerebrospinal fluid revealed no organisms. Whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography revealed no malignancy.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Abnormal enhancement of C1/C2 vertebrae with prevertebral and retrodental tissue as well as of the anterior vertebrae at C4/C5 with hyperostotic anterior osteophytes on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and multiple pustules on the palm (B).
case_info.explanation: D. Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. Current treatment options for SAPHO syndrome include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, and biologics.10 After oral etoricoxib and prednisolone treatment, neck pain and pustules gradually subsided and ESR and CRP decreased. The patient has remained clinically stable at 6-month follow-up. Clinicians should be aware of this unusual syndrome to avoid misdiagnosis (tumor/infection), unnecessary surgery, and antibiotic therapy.

case_info.caption: Abnormal enhancement of C1/C2 vertebrae with prevertebral and retrodental tissue as well as of the anterior vertebrae at C4/C5 with hyperostotic anterior osteophytes on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and multiple pustules on the palm (B).
case_info.explanation: D. Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. An association betweenCSF2RA,NOD2,MEGF6, andADAM5genes and the predisposition of SAPHO syndrome has been established.5Elevated serum IgG4 and some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL) 6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-23 and endothelin-1, have been described in patients with SAPHO syndrome.6In laboratory tests, and features of an active inflammatory process (accelerated ESR, elevated CRP) are observed.7 The diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome is based on fulfilling at least 1 of the criteria described by Kahn and Kahn,8which include (1) chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, usually sterile, spine may be involved, with or without skin lesions, (2) acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis associated with any of the following: palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), pustular psoriasis, or severe acne, and (3) any sterile osteitis associated with any of the following: PPP, pustular psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, or severe acne. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. Current treatment options for SAPHO syndrome include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, and biologics.10 After oral etoricoxib and prednisolone treatment, neck pain and pustules gradually subsided and ESR and CRP decreased. The patient has remained clinically stable at 6-month follow-up. Clinicians should be aware of this unusual syndrome to avoid misdiagnosis (tumor/infection), unnecessary surgery, and antibiotic therapy.

Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome Sudden rotation of the neck inducing a sharp pain on the side of the upper neck or occiput, followed immediately by transient numbness of the tongue on the same side is the character of neck-tongue syndrome, a uncommon headache syndrome.1The pain is related to an irritation of the C2 and/or C3 roots, with tongue involvement due to afferent impulses traveling from the lingual nerve via the hypoglossal nerve to the C1/C2 roots.2Abnormalities showed by magnetic resonance imaging in C1/C2 vertebrae were consistent with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis. Neurosyphilis (choice A), metastatic tumor (choice B), and rickettsial infection (choice C) were all excluded after the tests of rapid plasma reagin, rickettsial antibodies, and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography, respectively. Multiple pustules on the hand accompanying C1/C2 spondylitis and spondylodiscitis and tenderness in the right sternoclavicular articulation reminded us of suspicion of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. A whole-body bone scintigraphy was ordered, revealing the classic bull head sign with increased tracer uptake in bilateral sternoclavicular joints and the sternal angle (Figure 2), which is highly specific for SAPHO syndrome.3 First described by Chamot et al,4SAPHO syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease characterized by dermatological and osteoarticular symptoms. Infectious, genetic susceptibility, immunological, and environmental factors may play a role in the development of the disease. Propionibacterium acnes antigen has been only occasionally found in bacterial cultures. An association betweenCSF2RA,NOD2,MEGF6, andADAM5genes and the predisposition of SAPHO syndrome has been established.5Elevated serum IgG4 and some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL) 6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-23 and endothelin-1, have been described in patients with SAPHO syndrome.6In laboratory tests, and features of an active inflammatory process (accelerated ESR, elevated CRP) are observed.7 The diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome is based on fulfilling at least 1 of the criteria described by Kahn and Kahn,8which include (1) chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, usually sterile, spine may be involved, with or without skin lesions, (2) acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis associated with any of the following: palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), pustular psoriasis, or severe acne, and (3) any sterile osteitis associated with any of the following: PPP, pustular psoriasis, psoriasis vulgaris, or severe acne. Sternocostoclavicular osteitis and hyperostosis, spondyloarthritis with hyperostosis, and PPP are the most common triad of the disease occurring in adults.9As the osteoarticular and skin manifestations often do not occur simultaneously, the diagnosis can be difficult. As the cause is unknown, no consensus has been reached on the treatment of SAPHO syndrome. The primary goal of treatment is the improvement of clinical symptoms, thereby improving patients’ quality of life in the long term. Current treatment options for SAPHO syndrome include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, and biologics.10 After oral etoricoxib and prednisolone treatment, neck pain and pustules gradually subsided and ESR and CRP decreased. The patient has remained clinically stable at 6-month follow-up. Clinicians should be aware of this unusual syndrome to avoid misdiagnosis (tumor/infection), unnecessary surgery, and antibiotic therapy.
